meta.title: The A Form: Fewest New Notes, Biggest Change
meta.summary: The A form gains fewer new notes than any other CAGED window this chapter, and still loses its tidiness completely — the four it gains land on the two frets it used to skip entirely.

spans.text: . Sixteen dots — the fewest of the five windows — and only four of them new, also the fewest of any window this chapter adds. That's four fewer dots than the C form. It is also, for all that, the window these two notes change most: the four dots it gains are the ones that stop it fitting in three frets.
the tidiest and most regular on the whole neck: twelve dots inside three frets —
— with nothing at fret 4 and nothing at fret 6 at all. Two of the four new dots land on exactly those empty frets: a

, sits at the window's bottom fret. Chapter 3's tidiest window now uses every fret it has: frets 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 all carry something, where three of them used to be enough. Four dots, and two frets that held nothing before are suddenly in play.
Those two empty frets weren't ordinary empty frets, either. Fret 4 carries exactly one note of C major on the entire neck —

. In the first twelve frets those are the only two like that, and both happen to sit inside this one window. The single note on each is one this chapter adds — before now, frets 4 and 6 were genuinely bare.

Chapter 3 let you settle a hand across frets 2 to 5 and reach every dot in the window without moving. This window's new top fret, 6, sits one further out than that — the first dot in the A form that a comfortable four-fret hand position doesn't already cover.
Strings 1 and 6 are untouched. Both still carry exactly two dots — the

at fret 5 — the same content in the same places they've held since chapter 3. Every window except the C form has one string like that, but this is the only one with two, and they're a matched pair: chapter 1's fact showing up again, since strings 6 and 1 hold the same note at the same fret two octaves apart, so when one reads a certain way down its length, so does the other. Every other string in this window picked up something new; these two didn't.
Each new dot sits exactly where the opener's rule said it would.

. Two 3s and two roots, four new neighbours — the half-step rule landing in a real window for the first time. Compare it to the C form's six new dots and the difference in scale is obvious, even though the rule underneath both windows was identical.
Fewest new notes, biggest change — four dots put something on frets 4 and 6, which this window used to skip entirely, and push its reach out to five frets.

Chapter 3's fret-5 fact hasn't moved: one finger laid across fret 5 still catches six notes of the scale. What's changed is that fret 5 is no longer the only fret worth noticing in this window — the closer explains why it was ever alone in the first place.

Same window, fourth layer, and the last one there will be. Chapter 1 marked two roots in it, chapter 2 seven chord tones, chapter 3 twelve dots; sixteen is where it stops. The shape underneath has not moved a fret in four chapters.

props.caption: The A form's window at its fourth and final layer: sixteen dots across all five frets — the window chapter 3 called the tidiest of the five, now stretched to match the rest.
